claims.text: Adding a minor amount of boron to a metallic-glass alloy enhances its glass-forming ability.
Boron disrupts regular atomic packing in the alloy.
Boron increases the viscosity of the melt.
Packing disruption and increased melt viscosity suppress nucleation and crystallization during rapid cooling.
A boron concentration of approximately 1 wt% is an appropriate intervention for enhancing glass-forming ability.
Small boron atoms enhance icosahedral short-range order in the liquid alloy.
Boron is a small-sized metalloid relative to the alloy constituents.
Boron-induced local order delays or suppresses nucleation of crystalline phases during rapid cooling.
Boron-alloyed samples will contain a lower crystalline-phase fraction than boron-free controls.
Boron-alloyed samples will require a higher critical cooling rate to induce crystallization than boron-free controls.
Boron-free samples have a greater tendency to form crystalline phases under otherwise similar cooling conditions.
The magnitude of the boron effect depends on boron concentration and base-alloy composition.
Phase formation depends on the applied cooling rate.
The optimal boron concentration varies among alloy systems.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome specifies a higher critical cooling rate to induce crystallization, whereas the experiment proposes measuring the critical cooling rate required to achieve an amorphous structure. These are opposite endpoints, so the expected direction of the cooling-rate comparison is not consistently defined.
